interfaces.name: Goal and Human-Control API
interfaces.contract: Authenticated tenant context, goal, attachments, user constraints, plan-review response and correlation identifier; returns plan status, outcome or classified failure.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Goal submission is accepted once into a run state; repeated submissions require an idempotency key. Invalid identity, tenant or input is rejected. Orchestrator unavailability returns a retryable failure and creates no tool action.

interfaces.name: Identity Context Interface
interfaces.contract: Authenticated actor, tenant, service identity and authorization attributes with issuer and validity metadata.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Invalid, expired, missing or conflicting identity context fails closed; model- or user-supplied identity claims are not accepted as authoritative.
securityControls: Signed or otherwise verifiable identity context
No credentials in model context or logs

interfaces.name: Policy Decision Interface
interfaces.contract: Actor, tenant, purpose, plan version, task, requested capability, data classes and resource context; returns allow, deny or approval-required with reason and policy version.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: A missing, malformed, stale or unavailable decision results in deny or defer; no action authority is cached beyond its defined scope.

interfaces.name: Bounded Delegation Interface
interfaces.contract: Immutable task identifier, purpose, allowed capability set, scoped data references, run budget and correlation context; returns proposal, evidence or classified failure.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Delegation is at-least-once only where the task is side-effect-free and idempotent; duplicate proposals are deduplicated by task identifier. Timeout or malformed output terminates or replans the task without inheriting additional privilege.

interfaces.name: Model Invocation Interface
interfaces.owner: Model platform and model risk owners
interfaces.contract: Approved model-use purpose, minimized context, response schema, run identifier and resource policy; returns untrusted model output and usage metadata.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Timeout, refusal, invalid output or unavailable model returns a classified failure. Retries are bounded by run policy and cannot widen data or authority scope.

interfaces.name: Proposed Tool Action Interface
interfaces.contract: Plan and task version, actor, tenant, purpose, allowlisted operation, validated arguments, data classes, policy context and any approval reference.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: The gateway independently reauthorizes the current action. Missing policy, invalid arguments, stale plan or absent required approval is denied. A proposal is never evidence that an action occurred.

interfaces.name: Approval Request and Decision Interface
interfaces.contract: Human-readable action summary plus action digest, plan version, actor, tenant, purpose, tool operation, scope and impact classification; returns explicit approve, reject or expire evidence.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Pending approval causes no external action. Rejection, expiry, mismatch or service failure stops the action and returns an escalated state. Changed action content requires a new approval.

interfaces.name: Enterprise Tool Adapter Interface
interfaces.contract: Bounded operation-specific API using a scoped service identity, validated request, idempotency metadata where supported and correlation identifier.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Read and mutation semantics are declared per adapter. Unknown outcome after timeout is marked indeterminate and escalated rather than blindly retried. Retries are allowed only where the adapter contract establishes safety.

interfaces.name: Governed Memory Interface
interfaces.contract: Tenant, run, subject, purpose, memory type, classification, provenance and retention-policy reference; returns authorized records with trust labels.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Working-memory writes are run-scoped. Durable writes require applicable policy. Tenant or classification mismatch fails closed. Unavailable memory produces a classified failure or reduced-context mode only when policy permits.

interfaces.name: Audit and Telemetry Event Interface
interfaces.source: C-UX, C-ORCH, C-AGENT, C-MODEL, C-POLICY, C-TOOL, C-APPROVAL and C-MEMORY
interfaces.contract: Correlated event envelope containing event type, time, actor or service, tenant, run, plan and task references, decision or outcome, source and schema version.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Business execution must not silently discard required audit evidence. Delivery failure is buffered where safe, surfaced operationally and may stop high-impact execution when required evidence cannot be preserved. Duplicate events are tolerated by event identity.
securityControls: No secrets or unrestricted prompt capture

interfaces.name: Evaluation Interface
interfaces.contract: Approved, minimized evaluation samples and correlated outcomes with policy, model and prompt-template versions.
interfaces.consistencyAndFailureSemantics: Evaluation is asynchronous and cannot authorize actions. Missing or invalid samples are quarantined; evaluation failure raises an operational issue without rewriting original audit evidence.

dataArchitecture: Use a run identifier as the primary correlation boundary and immutable plan and task versions to distinguish proposals from authorized execution state.
Partition working memory by tenant and run; expire it under an approved retention policy and do not automatically promote it to durable memory.
Store durable memory separately with subject, purpose, classification, provenance, trust label, retention-policy reference and deletion status.

Treat user content, retrieved records, tool output and model output as untrusted content even when retrieved from an authenticated source; authority comes only from identity, policy and approval services.
Keep approval evidence bound to an action digest, plan version, actor, tenant, purpose, tool operation and scope so changed actions cannot reuse approval.
Record audit evidence for plan versions, delegations, policy decisions, approvals, tool attempts, externally reported outcomes and classified failures.
Do not place unrestricted prompts, secrets, credentials or raw sensitive tool payloads in telemetry; retain references or minimized evidence where reconstruction permits.
Define a human-approved data classification and retention matrix before durable-memory or evaluation-data production use.
securityArchitecture: Separate reasoning from authority: model and specialist outputs are proposals, while the orchestrator, policy engine, approval service and tool gateway control execution.
Issue distinct workload identities to the orchestrator, specialist runtime, model gateway and each tool adapter; do not share user or peer-agent credentials implicitly.
Deny direct network paths and credentials from model or specialist runtimes to enterprise mutation APIs.
Evaluate purpose, actor, tenant, data classification, tool operation, plan version and approval state at the action boundary.

Constrain prompt injection by isolating instructions from data, labeling untrusted content, validating outputs and prohibiting retrieved content from changing policy, identity, tool allowlists or approval requirements.
Enforce tenant scope in identity context, memory keys, authorization requests, telemetry access and evaluation exports.
Keep secrets in runtime secret facilities and outside prompts, memory payloads and audit events.
Require security and tool owners to review adapter contracts, service identities, allowlists and data flows before enabling each operation.
deploymentRuntime: Adopt candidate coarse service boundaries for orchestration, specialist execution, tool access, memory and audit/evaluation; policy, approval, identity, models and enterprise tools remain integrations.

Permit initial co-deployment of compatible control-plane components when operational maturity requires it, while preserving build-time boundaries and independent identities. This is a reversible candidate posture, not an approved style selection.
Place specialist and model-facing execution in a restricted zone without direct enterprise-tool mutation routes.
Place the Tool Gateway in a controlled integration zone with outbound access limited to allowlisted tool endpoints and identities.
Keep stateful memory and audit stores tenant-aware, encrypted and accessible only through their owning services.
Scale and isolate specialist execution by workload class; enforce policy-defined concurrency, iteration, elapsed-time and cost controls without asserting unsupplied numeric limits.
Use separate non-production environments and synthetic or approved test data for safety and failure testing.
Record deployment topology, ownership, rollback and recovery procedures before implementation handoff.
resilienceFailurePaths: Model timeout, refusal, malformed response or hallucination: reject invalid output, apply only policy-bounded retry or alternate-capability handling, then return a classified failure or human escalation.
Specialist failure: terminate the task scope, preserve evidence and prevent privilege or state from cascading to sibling capabilities.
Policy failure or indeterminate decision: deny or defer the requested capability or tool action; do not fall back to model judgment.
Approval failure, rejection or expiry: leave the external action unexecuted and expose a human-actionable state.
Tool validation or authorization failure: deny the call and record the policy and validation reason.
Tool timeout with unknown side-effect outcome: mark the action indeterminate, query status where the adapter supports it and otherwise escalate; do not blindly retry.
Memory failure: avoid cross-tenant or stale fallback. Continue with reduced context only when policy permits and clearly disclose the limitation.
Audit evidence delivery failure: buffer within governed limits and alert; stop high-impact execution if mandatory evidence cannot be captured.
Runaway loop or resource pressure: the orchestrator stops dispatch when configured run, iteration, elapsed-time, concurrency or cost policy is reached and escalates or returns a classified failure.
Control-plane overload: isolate specialist workloads from policy, approval, tool and audit components so execution demand cannot consume their protected capacity.

Recovery: back up and restore durable memory, approval references and audit evidence according to objectives still requiring human definition; test restoration and failover before production acceptance.
observabilityOperations: Propagate tenant-safe correlation across goal, run, plan, task, model call, policy decision, approval and tool action.
Expose operational signals for outcome class, model and tool failures, policy denials, approval queues, memory errors, audit-delivery health, latency, resource consumption and cost attribution.
Separate safety and quality evaluation from production authorization; evaluations may create findings but cannot approve tool actions.
Alert on repeated authorization denials, cross-tenant access attempts, unexpected tool operations, indeterminate side effects, exhausted run policy and missing required audit evidence.
Provide auditor views that reconstruct control decisions while enforcing evidence minimization and role-based access.
Maintain runbooks for model unavailability, policy outage, approval backlog, tool indeterminate outcome, memory recovery, suspected prompt injection and tenant-isolation incidents.
Define measurable service, safety, quality and cost objectives before production handoff; none are inferred in this candidate package.
transitionArchitecture: Phase 1: adjudicate duplicate requirement REQ-002/REQ-006, accept candidate journeys and define measurable quality scenarios.
Phase 2: materialize the canonical Design Graph and propose ADRs for style, control authority, tool boundary, identity isolation, memory, audit and recovery.
Phase 3: implement the governed orchestrator, identity context, policy integration and audit envelope without enabling mutating tool operations.
Phase 4: onboard read-only tool adapters with operation contracts, untrusted-content controls and failure tests.
Phase 5: add durable memory only after classification, purpose, retention and deletion policies are approved.
Phase 6: enable selected external mutations only after tool-owner review, deterministic policy, approval binding and indeterminate-outcome handling are tested.
Phase 7: conduct recovery, isolation, injection, runaway-loop, audit-reconstruction and human-control exercises before any production acceptance.

Rollback posture: disable affected tool operations and specialist capabilities through deterministic configuration, preserve evidence and retain the user-facing system in non-mutating or read-only mode where policy permits.

decisions.title: Use coarse service-based boundaries with reversible deployment
decisions.selectedOption: Candidate service-based separation for orchestrator, specialist runtime, tool gateway, memory and audit/evaluation, allowing initial co-deployment where boundaries and identities remain enforceable.
alternatives: Microservices for every specialist and control capability
Single undifferentiated application process
Event-driven decomposition as the primary application style
decisions.rationale: The AIW deterministic recommendation identifies Service-Based as eligible but weak and requires adoption preconditions, rollback and ownership. Distributed alternatives are not supported for this architecture stage, no calibrated quality-driver weights exist, and no accepted asynchronous journeys justify event-driven primacy.
tradeoffs: Coarse boundaries improve ownership and failure containment but add integration and operational work.
Co-deployment reduces early operating burden but limits independent scaling and requires build-time boundary enforcement.
Later extraction remains possible but requires stable contracts and telemetry.
consequences: Document owners, monitoring, failure handling, adoption preconditions and rollback.
Do not interpret this candidate as an approved pattern or deployment decision.
Reassess if team ownership, operational maturity or independent scaling needs materially change.

decisions.title: Separate probabilistic planning from deterministic run control
decisions.selectedOption: Models may propose plans or task outputs, but a deterministic orchestrator validates plan structure, maintains authoritative run state and enforces policy-defined execution limits.
alternatives: Allow an autonomous agent to own run state and execute actions
Use only deterministic workflows with no model planning
Let each specialist independently coordinate peers
decisions.rationale: AA-FR-001 requires governed decomposition, while AA-C-001 and AA-C-002 deny model mutation authority and require deterministic policy for high-impact actions. The AIW requirements-taxonomy and conflict-detection outputs preserve these constraints as explicit design inputs.
tradeoffs: Improves control and auditability at the cost of orchestration complexity.
Restricts adaptive behavior that cannot be represented within the governed task contract.
Deterministic workflows alone would reduce model risk but may not satisfy the intended agentic coordination objective.
consequences: Every task and plan is versioned and validated.
Model output never serves as policy, identity, approval or execution evidence.
Run limits and failure states require human-owned definitions.

decisions.title: Isolate specialist and tool privileges
decisions.selectedOption: Give each specialist capability a task-scoped context and workload identity; keep all enterprise tool credentials in operation-specific Tool Gateway adapters.
alternatives: Share the orchestrator identity with all specialists
Delegate the end-user credential to specialists
Give each specialist direct tool credentials
decisions.rationale: AA-FR-002 prohibits implicit privilege sharing, AA-QR-003 requires least privilege and tenant isolation, and AA-C-001 prohibits direct model or agent mutation.
tradeoffs: Stronger isolation increases identity, policy and adapter administration.
Centralized adapters may add latency and become a protected dependency.
Direct credentials would simplify integration but violate the supplied authority boundary.
consequences: Specialists cannot call enterprise mutation endpoints directly.
Tool authorization is operation-specific and independently evaluated.
Network policy must enforce the logical restriction.

decisions.title: Make the Tool Gateway the exclusive external-action boundary
decisions.selectedOption: Route every enterprise tool operation through allowlisted adapters that re-evaluate deterministic policy and require action-bound human approval when classified as high-impact.
alternatives: Allow orchestrator or agents to call tools directly
Approve whole plans instead of individual high-impact actions
Rely on tool-side authorization without an application action boundary
decisions.rationale: Directly implements AA-FR-003, AA-FR-005, AA-C-001 and AA-C-002. The open duplicate REQ-002/REQ-006 does not change the scenario constraint but its provenance must be adjudicated.
tradeoffs: Central enforcement improves consistency and evidence but creates a critical dependency.
Action-bound approval limits approval reuse but may increase human workload.
Tool-side authorization remains necessary but is insufficient to enforce application purpose and plan context.
consequences: Policy or approval uncertainty fails closed.
Approval is invalidated when material action content changes.
Each adapter must declare side-effect and retry semantics.

decisions.title: Separate working memory from durable memory
decisions.selectedOption: Use run-scoped ephemeral working memory and a separate durable store whose writes and reads require classification, purpose, tenant, provenance and retention policy.
alternatives: Use one unrestricted conversation and memory store
Keep no durable memory
Let models decide what should be retained
decisions.rationale: AA-FR-004 requires governed working and durable memory, while AA-QR-003 requires classification and tenant isolation. The source-evidence-contract rule supports preserving provenance rather than treating generated summaries as authoritative evidence.
tradeoffs: Separation reduces accidental retention but adds lifecycle and retrieval complexity.
No durable memory would reduce privacy exposure but may not meet the functional requirement.
Policy-controlled writes can reduce convenience and recall.
consequences: Working memory is not automatically promoted.
Durable memory remains blocked from production use until retention and deletion rules are defined.
Retrieved memory is labeled as untrusted content.

decisions.title: Apply an untrusted-content boundary to every model-facing input and output
decisions.selectedOption: Keep instructions, authority and tool contracts separate from user, retrieved, model and tool content; label content, minimize context and validate structured outputs before use.
alternatives: Trust authenticated enterprise content
Use prompt instructions as the only injection defense
Block all retrieved and tool content from models
decisions.rationale: AA-QR-001 and the supplied untrusted-input constraint explicitly require resistance to prompt injection. AIW source-evidence-contract and unsupported-metric-guard rules support provenance and rejection of unsupported claims rather than implicit trust.
tradeoffs: Validation and context isolation reduce flexibility and increase implementation effort.
Content labeling cannot eliminate all model error, so authority boundaries remain necessary.
Blocking all external content would materially reduce utility.
consequences: Retrieved content cannot alter identity, policy, allowlists or approval rules.
Invalid structured output becomes a classified failure or re-planning input.
Injection testing is required for each tool and retrieval path.

decisions.title: Use a correlated audit and evaluation plane without execution authority
decisions.selectedOption: Capture append-oriented, correlated evidence for plans, delegation, policy, approvals, tool attempts and outcomes; expose minimized copies to observability and evaluation.
alternatives: Log only final user-visible outcomes
Allow each component to keep unrelated local logs
Use evaluation results to automatically authorize actions
decisions.rationale: AA-FR-006 and AA-QR-004 require end-to-end audit and observation. The architecture review also identifies missing ADR coverage, so this remains a proposed decision rather than an approved fact.
tradeoffs: Comprehensive evidence improves reconstruction but increases sensitive-data and retention risk.
Central correlation adds dependency and schema governance.
Evaluation separated from authorization prevents feedback from directly widening authority.
consequences: Audit schemas require versioning and ownership.
Required evidence delivery failures are operationally visible and may block high-impact execution.
Prompt and payload capture must be minimized.

decisions.title: Record and test recovery for governed state
decisions.selectedOption: Define backup, restoration, failover and reconciliation procedures for durable memory, approval references, run state and audit evidence, with objectives supplied by accountable owners.
alternatives: Rely only on underlying platform defaults
Recover audit and memory independently without reconciliation
Defer recovery design until production
decisions.rationale: AIW deterministic finding GOV-RECOVERY-DECISION requires an accepted recovery decision covering backup, failover and recovery testing. No recovery objectives are supplied, so the candidate abstains from inventing them.
tradeoffs: Recovery testing adds operational effort and controlled interruption.
Cross-store reconciliation is more complex than isolated restoration.
Platform defaults may be useful implementation mechanisms but do not establish business recovery intent.
consequences: Production handoff remains blocked until objectives, owners and test evidence exist.
Recovery must preserve tenant boundaries and approval-to-action lineage.
Indeterminate external side effects require tool-specific reconciliation.

risks.description: Prompt injection or hostile retrieved/tool content influences planning or attempts to redefine authority.
risks.mitigation: Separate instructions from data, label provenance, minimize context, validate outputs, test injection paths and enforce authority outside the model.

risks.description: Excessive agency or delegation causes an agent to exceed task, policy or approval scope.
risks.mitigation: Use deterministic run control, task-scoped capability grants, independent policy checks, bounded execution and human escalation.

risks.description: Sensitive or cross-tenant data leaks through context, memory, telemetry, evaluation or shared identities.
risks.mitigation: Enforce tenant-bound identity and storage keys, classification policy, least-data context, access controls, redaction and controlled evaluation exports.

risks.description: A tool is misused through an unauthorized operation, manipulated arguments or over-privileged service identity.
risks.mitigation: Use operation allowlists, adapter validation, purpose-bound policy, scoped service identities, action-bound approval and tool-owner review.

risks.description: Planning or specialist delegation enters a runaway loop.
risks.mitigation: Enforce configured iteration, recursion, elapsed-time and concurrency policy in the orchestrator and escalate on exhaustion.

risks.description: Model or tool use causes uncontrolled cost or latency.
risks.mitigation: Apply purpose-aware model routing, configured resource budgets, usage correlation, bounded retries and termination or approval when policy is reached.

risks.description: Delegation, policy, approval and tool outcomes cannot be reconstructed consistently.
risks.mitigation: Use immutable identifiers and versions, correlated audit envelopes, approval-to-action binding, event integrity and audit reconstruction tests.

risks.description: Model, policy, approval, memory, audit or tool dependency failure cascades across active runs.
risks.mitigation: Use isolation, protected control-plane capacity, fail-closed action paths, classified failures, bounded retries and run-level containment.

risks.description: Audit, memory or evaluation retention creates unnecessary sensitive-data exposure.
risks.mitigation: Define data-class retention and deletion policy, minimize payloads, restrict access and prevent automatic promotion from working to durable stores.

risks.description: Undefined recovery objectives or untested restoration cause loss, inconsistency or unavailable governed evidence.
risks.mitigation: Assign recovery owners, define objectives, record a recovery ADR and test backup, restore, failover and cross-store reconciliation.

delivery.executiveSummary: This candidate architecture separates probabilistic reasoning from deterministic authority. A governed orchestrator coordinates isolated specialist capabilities; a deterministic policy point, action-bound approval service and exclusive Tool Gateway control enterprise actions. Working and durable memory are separated by tenant, purpose, classification and retention policy, while a correlated audit and evaluation plane supports reconstruction and operations. The package remains unaccepted because high-impact classification, data lifecycle rules, measurable quality scenarios, recovery objectives, canonical graph materialization and ADR approval require human decisions.

sddSections.heading: Architecture Style and Boundaries
sddSections.content: Use coarse service-based boundaries as a reversible candidate. Preserve separate ownership, identities and contracts even if some control components are initially co-deployed. Do not adopt microservices or event-driven primacy without accepted operational and journey evidence.

sddSections.heading: Agent and Orchestration Model
sddSections.content: The orchestrator owns authoritative run and plan state. Specialist capabilities receive one bounded task, scoped context and identity. Model and specialist outputs are proposals and cannot establish identity, policy, approval or tool authority.

sddSections.heading: Tool and Approval Control
sddSections.content: All tool calls pass through operation-specific adapters. The gateway validates inputs, rechecks deterministic policy and holds high-impact actions for explicit, action-bound approval. Unknown side-effect outcomes are escalated rather than blindly retried.

sddSections.heading: Memory and Data Governance
sddSections.content: Working memory is ephemeral and run-scoped. Durable memory requires classification, purpose, provenance, tenant and retention policy. Retrieved memory and tool content remain untrusted. Production use depends on an approved data lifecycle matrix.

sddSections.heading: Security and Failure Containment
sddSections.content: Distinct identities, restricted network paths, externalized authority and fail-closed control dependencies contain agent failure. Bounded execution, protected control-plane capacity and explicit indeterminate states address loops, outages and tool uncertainty.

sddSections.heading: Audit, Evaluation and Operations
sddSections.content: Correlated evidence covers plans, delegation, policy, approvals, tool calls and outcomes. Telemetry observes quality, safety, latency, cost and control decisions, but evaluations cannot authorize actions. Sensitive payload capture is minimized.

sddSections.heading: Governance Posture
sddSections.content: AIW deterministic analysis reports an open duplicate requirement conflict, missing ADR coverage, no accepted pattern, incomplete measurable quality scenarios and a required recovery decision. All architecture records in this package are proposals and change no approved state.
